results.assessment_question: Does the framework define retention requirements for serious-incident documentation that meet or exceed a five-year period?
expected_evidence: The framework states that documentation of information related to serious incidents must be retained.
The framework specifies a minimum retention period of at least five years.
The framework indicates that the retention period is counted from the later of the documentation date or the date of the serious incident.
Indicative keywords/phrases: retain, retention, serious incident, documentation, records, five years, minimum period, archival, storage

Signatories commit to documenting the implementation of this Chapter (as specified in Measure 10.1)

Further, Signatories will keep track of the following information, to the extent it is not already covered 
by the first paragraph, for the purpose of evidencing adherence to this Chapter to the AI Office upon 
request: 
(1) their processes, measures, and key decisions that form part of their systemic risk assessment 
and mitigation; and

third paragraph), including that the systemic risks stemming from the model have been

architectural details, capabilities, propensities, affordances, and safety mitigations. Such

and/or security mitigations and to protect sensitive commercial information. For Model Reports, such 
publication will include high-level descriptions of the systemic risk assessment results and the safety 
and security mitigations implemented. For Frameworks, such publication is not necessary if all of the 
Signatory’s models are similarly safe or safer models pursuant to Appendix 2.2. For Model Reports, 
such publication is not necessary if the model is a similarly safe or safer model pursuant to Appendix 
2.2.

A Framework assessment will include the following: 
(1) Framework adequacy: An assessment of whether the processes and measures in the 
Framework are appropriate for the systemic risks stemming from the Signatories’ models. 
This assessment will take into account how the models are currently being developed,  
made available on the market, and/or used, and how they are expected to be developed, 
made available on the market, and/or used over the next 12 months. 
(2) Framework adherence: An assessment focused on the Signatories’ adherence to the 
Framework, including: (a) any instances of, and reasons for, non-adherence to the Framework 
since the last Framework assessment; and (b) any measures, including safety and security 
mitigations, that need to be implemented to ensure continued adherence to the Framework. 
If point(s) (a) and/or (b) give rise to risks of future non-adherence, Signatories will make 
remediation plans as part of their Framework assessment.

criteria.requirement: Define a state-of-the-art Safety and Security Framework that conceptually describes how systemic risks are assessed, accepted, and mitigated across the model lifecycle.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework define, at a conceptual and descriptive level, the key elements required for systemic risk management under the Safety and Security Chapter (including trigger points, risk acceptance logic, mitigation expectations, responsibility allocation, external input, and update processes)?
expected_evidence: The framework explicitly describes its purpose as managing systemic risks associated with general-purpose AI models.
The framework outlines how systemic risks are identified, assessed, and mitigated at a high level.
The framework describes trigger points at which additional evaluations or assessments would occur during the model lifecycle.
The framework defines how systemic risk acceptability is determined, including the use of risk tiers or acceptance criteria.
The framework describes, at a high level, expected categories or types of safety and security mitigations associated with different risk levels.
The framework explains how responsibility for systemic risk assessment and mitigation is allocated within the organization.
The framework describes whether and how input from external actors may influence risk-related decisions.
The framework describes how and under what conditions the framework itself would be reviewed or updated.

Signatories will implement the processes and measures outlined in their Framework as specified in 
the following paragraphs. 
Along the entire model lifecycle, Signatories will continuously:

automated evaluations) at appropriate trigger points defined in terms of, e.g. time, 
training compute, development stages, user access, inference compute, and/or

implementing safety and/or security mitigations as specified in Commitments 5 and 6, and 
re-assessing the systemic risks stemming from the model starting from point (1), as specified 
in Measure 4.2.

placing the model on the market and whenever the conditions specified in Measure 7.6, first and 
third paragraph, are met. Signatories will report their implemented measures and processes to the

criteria.title: Framework updates
criteria.requirement: Describe how the Safety and Security Framework defines the conditions, processes, and scope for periodic and event-driven framework assessments and updates, including versioning, changelogs, and remediation planning, in line with Measure 1.3 of the Safety and Security Chapter.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework define how and when framework assessments and updates are intended to occur, including assessment triggers, periodic review, evaluation of framework adequacy and adherence, and the handling of remediation and versioning?
expected_evidence: The framework describes that it is subject to periodic reassessment (e.g. at defined intervals) and to reassessment when specified conditions or events occur.

The framework describes conditions or triggers that would lead to a framework assessment (e.g. material changes in model development, serious incidents or near misses, materially changed systemic risks or model capabilities).
The framework explains the scope of a framework assessment, including the evaluation of framework adequacy with respect to the systemic risks of the models.
The framework explains that framework adherence is assessed, including consideration of non-adherence and its causes.
The framework describes how findings from a framework assessment may lead to updates of the framework to keep it state-of-the-art.
The framework describes that updates are intended to be versioned and accompanied by a changelog explaining the nature and rationale of changes.
The framework describes how remediation plans are intended to be defined when framework assessments identify risks of continued or future non-adherence.
Indicative concepts and phrases: framework assessment, adequacy, adherence, periodic review, reassessment triggers, serious incidents, material changes, versioning, changelog, remediation planning
criteria.reasoning: Most indicators are present: periodic reassessment, event-driven triggers (material changes, serious incidents, changing systemic risks), evaluation of framework adequacy and adherence, remediation planning, and versioning with a changelog and an update/confirmation process. However, the text lacks an explicit statement that assessment findings will drive updates to keep the framework state-of-the-art, which is required to fully satisfy the expected evidence. This gap addresses indicator related to proactive, state-of-the-art updates and cannot be offset by thematic alignment alone.

Commitment 1 Safety and Security Framework 
 
LEGAL TEXT: Articles 55(1) and 56(5), and recitals 110, 114, and 115 AI Act 
 
Signatories commit to adopting a state-of-the-art Safety and Security Framework (“Framework”). The 
purpose of the Framework is to outline the systemic risk management processes and measures that 
Signatories implement to ensure the systemic risks stemming from their models are acceptable.  
 
Signatories commit to a Framework adoption process that involves three steps: 
(1) creating the Framework (as specified in Measure 1.1); 
(2) implementing the Framework (as specified in Measure 1.2); and 
(3) updating the Framework (as specified in Measure 1.3). 
 
Further, Signatories commit to notifying the AI Office of their Framework (as specified in Measure 
1.4). 
 
Figure 1. Process for creating, implementing, and updating Frameworks.  
The text of the Commitments and Measures takes precedence. 
Measure 1.1 Creating the Framework 
Signatories will create a state-of-the-art Framework, taking into account the models they are 
developing, making available on the market, and/or using. 
The Framework will contain a high-level description of implemented and planned processes and 
measures for systemic risk assessment and mitigation to adhere to this Chapter. 
In addition, the Framework will contain: 
(1) a description and justification of the trigger points and their usage, at which the Signatories

(d) a description of whether and, if so, by what process input from external actors, 
including governments, influences proceeding with the development, making 
available on the market, and/or use of the Signatories’ models as specified in 
Measure 4.2, other than as the result of independent external evaluations; 
(3) a description of how systemic risk responsibility is allocated for the processes by which 
systemic risk is assessed and mitigated as specified in Commitment 8; and 
(4) a description of the process by which Signatories will update the Framework, including how 
they will determine that an updated Framework is confirmed, as specified in Measure 1.3. 
Signatories will have confirmed the Framework no later than four weeks after having notified the 
Commission pursuant to Article 52(1) AI Act and no later than two weeks before placing the model 
on the market. 
Measure 1.2 Implementing the Framework 
Signatories will implement the processes and measures outlined in their Framework as specified in 
the following paragraphs. 
Along the entire model lifecycle, Signatories will continuously: 
(1) assess the systemic risks stemming from the model by: 
(a) conducting lighter-touch model evaluations that need not adhere to Appendix 3 (e.g. 
automated evaluations) at appropriate trigger points defined in terms of, e.g. time, 
training compute, development stages, user access, inference compute, and/or 
affordances;

not changed since they have last provided the AI Office with the Model Report, or update thereof; (2) 
they will place a more capable model on the market in less than a month; and/or (3) the model is 
considered similarly safe or safer (pursuant to Appendix 2.2) for each identified systemic risk 
(pursuant to Measure 2.1).  
The updated Model Report will contain:  
(1) the updated information specified in Measures 7.1 to 7.5 based on the results of the full 
systemic risk assessment and mitigation process (pursuant to Measure 1.2, third paragraph); 
and 
(2) a changelog, describing how and why the Model Report has been updated, along with a 
version number and the date of change. 
Measure 7.7 Model Report notifications  
Signatories will provide the AI Office with access to the Model Report (without redactions, unless they 
are required by national security laws to which Signatories are subject) by the time they place a model 
on the market, e.g. through a publicly accessible link or through a sufficiently secure channel specified 
by the AI Office. If a Model Report is updated, Signatories will provide the AI Office with access to the 
updated Model Report (without redactions, unless they are required by national security laws to 
which Signatories are subject) within five business days of a confirmed update.

criteria.title: Risk identification process
criteria.requirement: Define a structured systemic risk identification process that is explicitly informed by the types of risks, the nature of systemic risks, and the sources of systemic risks as set out in Appendix 1, and that explicitly considers the specified systemic risks.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework define a structured systemic risk identification process that is informed by the risk types (Appendix 1.1), the nature of systemic risks (Appendix 1.2), the sources of systemic risks (Appendix 1.3), and that explicitly considers the specified systemic risks (Appendix 1.4)?
expected_evidence: The framework describes a structured process for identifying systemic risks stemming from the model.

The framework indicates that potential systemic risks are initially considered with reference to the types of risks defined in Appendix 1.1 (e.g. risks to public health, safety, public security, fundamental rights, and society).

The framework explains that the identification process considers the nature of systemic risks, including essential and contributing characteristics such as scale, propagation, capability-dependence, or irreversibility (Appendix 1.2).

The framework describes how potential sources of systemic risks are considered in the identification process, including model capabilities, model propensities, and model affordances or contextual factors (Appendix 1.3).

The framework explicitly indicates that the specified systemic risks listed in Appendix 1.4 are taken into account as part of the systemic risk identification process, such as risks related to chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) threats, loss of control of the model, large-scale cyber offence, and harmful manipulation.

Indicative concepts and phrases: systemic risk identification, structured process, risk types, nature of systemic risks, risk sources, model capabilities, model propensities, model affordances, specified systemic risks
criteria.reasoning: The framework establishes a structured systemic risk identification process and references Appendix 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, and 1.4 for risk types, nature, sources, and specified risks, and it includes risk scenarios (2.2). However, it does not explicitly require consideration of model capabilities, propensities, and affordances as risk sources (Appendix 1.3); it relies on generic model information rather than explicit sourcing elements, which leaves a gap relative to the Appendix 1.3 scope.

Appendix 1.2 Nature of systemic risks

Act.

(3) Said impact can be propagated at scale across the value chain pursuant to Article 3(65) AI 
Act.

(1) Capability-dependent: The risk increases with model capabilities or may emerge at the 
frontier of model capabilities.

In addition, the Framework will contain: 
(1) a description and justification of the trigger points and their usage, at which the Signatories 
will conduct additional lighter-touch model evaluations along the entire model lifecycle, as 
specified in Measure 1.2, second paragraph, point (1)(a);
(2) for the Signatories’ determination of whether systemic risk is considered acceptable, as 
specified in Commitment 4: 
(a) a description and justification of the systemic risk acceptance criteria, including the 
systemic risk tiers, and their usage as specified in Measure 4.1; 
(b) a high-level description of what safety and security mitigations Signatories would 
need to implement once each systemic risk tier is reached; 
(c) for each systemic risk that Signatories defined systemic risk tiers for as specified in 
Measure 4.1, estimates of timelines when Signatories reasonably foresee that they 
will have a model that exceeds the highest systemic risk tier already reached by any 
of their existing models. Such estimates: (i) may consist of time ranges or probability 
distributions; and (ii) may take into account aggregate forecasts, surveys, and other 
estimates produced with other providers. Further, such estimates will be supported 
by justifications, including underlying assumptions and uncertainties; and 
(d) a description of whether and, if so, by what process input from external actors, 
including governments, influences proceeding with the development, making

market, and/or the use of the model based on the systemic risk acceptance determination (as 
specified in Measure 4.2). 
Measure 4.1 Systemic risk acceptance criteria and acceptance determination 
Signatories will describe and justify (in the Framework pursuant to Measure 1.1, point (2)(a)) how 
they will determine whether the systemic risks stemming from the model are acceptable. To do so, 
Signatories will: 
(1) for each identified systemic risk (pursuant to Measure 2.1), at least: 
(a) define appropriate systemic risk tiers that: 
(i) 
are defined in terms of model capabilities, and may additionally incorporate 
model propensities, risk estimates, and/or other suitable metrics;  
(ii) 
are measurable; and 
(iii) 
comprise at least one systemic risk tier that has not been reached by the 
model; or 
(b) define other appropriate systemic risk acceptance criteria, if systemic risk tiers are 
not suitable for the systemic risk and the systemic risk is not a specified systemic risk 
(pursuant to Appendix 1.4); 
(2) describe how they will use these tiers and/or other criteria to determine whether each 
identified systemic risk (pursuant to Measure 2.1) and the overall systemic risk are 
acceptable; and
(3) justify how the use of these tiers and/or other criteria pursuant to point (2) ensures that each 
identified systemic risk (pursuant to Measure 2.1) and the overall systemic risk are 
acceptable.

A Framework assessment will include the following: 
(1) Framework adequacy: An assessment of whether the processes and measures in the 
Framework are appropriate for the systemic risks stemming from the Signatories’ models. 
This assessment will take into account how the models are currently being developed,  
made available on the market, and/or used, and how they are expected to be developed, 
made available on the market, and/or used over the next 12 months. 
(2) Framework adherence: An assessment focused on the Signatories’ adherence to the 
Framework, including: (a) any instances of, and reasons for, non-adherence to the Framework 
since the last Framework assessment; and (b) any measures, including safety and security 
mitigations, that need to be implemented to ensure continued adherence to the Framework. 
If point(s) (a) and/or (b) give rise to risks of future non-adherence, Signatories will make 
remediation plans as part of their Framework assessment.

Signatories will provide the AI Office with (unredacted) access to their Framework, and updates 
thereof, within five business days of either being confirmed.

criteria.title: Model-independent information
criteria.requirement: Describe how the framework defines the gathering of model-independent information relevant to systemic risk analysis, including how the breadth and depth of information gathering are determined in relation to the systemic risk.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the organisation systematically gather and document model-independent information relevant to identified systemic risks, using structured methods such as web searches or OSINT, literature reviews, market analyses of comparable models, training data reviews, historical incident analysis, forecasting of technological trends, expert consultations, and/or stakeholder or community engagement?
expected_evidence: The framework describes that systemic risk analysis is informed by model-independent information.
The framework explains that the breadth and depth of model-independent information gathering are adjusted based on the characteristics or severity of the systemic risk.

The framework indicates categories of methods that may be used to gather model-independent information, such as web searches or open-source intelligence, literature reviews, market analyses, reviews of historical incident data, forecasting of general trends, expert interviews or panels, and participatory or community-based research methods.

The framework clarifies the role of model-independent information in informing subsequent stages of systemic risk analysis (e.g. evaluations, modelling, or estimation), without requiring that such stages have already been performed.

Indicative concepts and phrases: model-independent information, information gathering, breadth and depth, proportionality, literature review, market analysis, incident data, expert input, participatory methods
criteria.reasoning: The indicators are largely present: the framework requires model-independent information gathering, proportional breadth/depth, enumerates methods (OSINT, literature reviews, market analyses, training data reviews, incident data, trend forecasting, expert input, participatory methods), and states information informs evaluations. However, explicit documentation/traceability requirements, concrete operational criteria for breadth/depth based on risk characteristics, and a direct, explicit linkage showing how model-independent information informs modelling and estimation (beyond evaluations) are missing. These gaps cannot be offset by thematic alignment alone.
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Explicit documentation/traceability requirements for model-independent information (sources used, dates, methods, decision logs).
Explicit, operational criteria or thresholds for determining breadth and depth of information gathering based on systemic risk characteristics.

Direct, explicit linkage showing how model-independent information informs modelling (Measure 3.3) and estimation (Measure 3.4) in addition to informing evaluations, including sequencing or flow of information across measures.
Lack of explicit retention, governance, or update cadence for the model-independent information gathered (e.g., how often sources are revisited or renewed).
Binding guidance on documentation and traceability of information sources and methods across all information-gathering activities.

Measure 3.2 Model evaluations  
Signatories will conduct at least state-of-the-art model evaluations in the modalities relevant to the 
systemic risk to assess the model’s capabilities, propensities, affordances, and/or effects, as specified 
in Appendix 3. 
Signatories will ensure that such model evaluations are designed and conducted using methods that

improve the understanding of the systemic risk, with a view to identifying unexpected behaviours,
capability boundaries, or emergent properties. Examples of model evaluation methods are: Q&A sets, 
task-based evaluations, benchmarks, red-teaming and other methods of adversarial testing, human 
uplift studies, model organisms, simulations, and/or proxy evaluations for classified materials.

Commitment 3 Systemic risk analysis 
 
LEGAL TEXT: Article 55(1) and recital 114 AI Act 
Signatories commit to analysing each identified systemic risk (pursuant to Commitment 2). The 
purpose of systemic risk analysis includes facilitating systemic risk acceptance determination 
(pursuant to Commitment 4).

Commitment 3 Systemic risk analysis 
 
LEGAL TEXT: Article 55(1) and recital 114 AI Act 
Signatories commit to analysing each identified systemic risk (pursuant to Commitment 2). The 
purpose of systemic risk analysis includes facilitating systemic risk acceptance determination 
(pursuant to Commitment 4). 
Systemic risk analysis involves five elements for each identified systemic risk, which may overlap and 
may need to be implemented recursively: 
(1) gathering model-independent information (as specified in Measure 3.1); 
(2) conducting model evaluations (as specified in Measure 3.2); 
(3) modelling the systemic risk (as specified in Measure 3.3); and 
(4) estimating the systemic risk (as specified in Measure 3.4); while 
(5) conducting post-market monitoring (as specified in Measure 3.5).  
Measure 3.1 Model-independent information 
Signatories will gather model-independent information relevant to the systemic risk. 
Signatories will search for and gather such information with varying degrees of breadth and depth 
appropriate for the systemic risk, using methods such as:  
(1) web searches (e.g. making use of open-source intelligence methods in collecting and 
analysing information gathered from open sources); 
(2) literature reviews; 
(3) market analyses (e.g. focused on capabilities of other models available on the market);  
(4) reviews of training data (e.g. for indications of data poisoning or tampering);

to the Signatory by the AI Office, the Scientific Panel of Independent Experts, 
or other initiatives, such as the International Network of AI Safety Institutes, 
endorsed for this purpose by the AI Office; 
(b) analysing relevant characteristics of the risks compiled pursuant to point (a), such as 
their nature (based on Appendix 1.2) and sources (based on Appendix 1.3); and  
(c) identifying, based on point (b), the systemic risks stemming from the model; and 
(2) the specified systemic risks in Appendix 1.4. 
Measure 2.2 Systemic risk scenarios 
Signatories will develop appropriate systemic risk scenarios, including regarding the number and level 
of detail of these systemic risk scenarios, for each identified systemic risk (pursuant to Measure 2.1).

In addition, the Framework will contain: 
(1) a description and justification of the trigger points and their usage, at which the Signatories 
will conduct additional lighter-touch model evaluations along the entire model lifecycle, as 
specified in Measure 1.2, second paragraph, point (1)(a);
(2) for the Signatories’ determination of whether systemic risk is considered acceptable, as 
specified in Commitment 4: 
(a) a description and justification of the systemic risk acceptance criteria, including the 
systemic risk tiers, and their usage as specified in Measure 4.1; 
(b) a high-level description of what safety and security mitigations Signatories would 
need to implement once each systemic risk tier is reached; 
(c) for each systemic risk that Signatories defined systemic risk tiers for as specified in 
Measure 4.1, estimates of timelines when Signatories reasonably foresee that they 
will have a model that exceeds the highest systemic risk tier already reached by any 
of their existing models. Such estimates: (i) may consist of time ranges or probability 
distributions; and (ii) may take into account aggregate forecasts, surveys, and other 
estimates produced with other providers. Further, such estimates will be supported 
by justifications, including underlying assumptions and uncertainties; and 
(d) a description of whether and, if so, by what process input from external actors, 
including governments, influences proceeding with the development, making

criteria.title: Risk estimation
criteria.requirement: Describe how the framework defines the estimation of the probability and severity of harm for systemic risks, using at least state-of-the-art risk estimation methods and taking into account relevant information inputs.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework describe how the probability and severity of harm for systemic risks are intended to be estimated using state-of-the-art methods, taking into account relevant information from systemic risk identification, analysis, and serious incident reporting, and how such estimates are expressed?
expected_evidence: The framework describes that probability and severity of harm are estimated as part of systemic risk analysis.
The framework indicates that at least state-of-the-art risk estimation methods are used, appropriate to the systemic risk being assessed.

The framework explains that risk estimation takes into account relevant information inputs, such as outputs from systemic risk identification and analysis and information about serious incidents or near misses.

The framework describes how estimates of systemic risk are expressed, for example as risk scores, risk matrices, probability distributions, or other qualitative, semi-quantitative, or quantitative formats.
The framework explains the purpose of risk estimation in supporting systemic risk acceptance determination, without requiring specific numerical or qualitative results.
Indicative concepts and phrases: systemic risk estimation, probability of harm, severity of harm, risk estimation methods, risk score, risk matrix, probability distribution
criteria.reasoning: All indicators in the Expected Evidence are present: probability and severity estimation as part of systemic risk analysis; use of state-of-the-art risk estimation methods with inputs from systemic risk identification and incident information; expressions of risk as risk scores/matrices/probability distributions; and the purpose to support systemic risk acceptance. No operational gaps or alignment_overreach were identified that would necessitate deeming any indicator unmet.

risk expression formats (risk score, risk matrix, probability distribution)
support for systemic risk acceptance determination

If and insofar as necessary to assess and/or mitigate systemic risks, Signatories will publish (e.g. via 
their websites) a summarised version of their Framework and Model Report(s), and updates thereof

Measure 4.1 Systemic risk acceptance criteria and acceptance determination 
Signatories will describe and justify (in the Framework pursuant to Measure 1.1, point (2)(a)) how 
they will determine whether the systemic risks stemming from the model are acceptable. To do so, 
Signatories will: 
(1) for each identified systemic risk (pursuant to Measure 2.1), at least: 
(a) define appropriate systemic risk tiers that: 
(i) 
are defined in terms of model capabilities, and may additionally incorporate 
model propensities, risk estimates, and/or other suitable metrics;  
(ii) 
are measurable; and 
(iii) 
comprise at least one systemic risk tier that has not been reached by the 
model; or 
(b) define other appropriate systemic risk acceptance criteria, if systemic risk tiers are 
not suitable for the systemic risk and the systemic risk is not a specified systemic risk 
(pursuant to Appendix 1.4); 
(2) describe how they will use these tiers and/or other criteria to determine whether each 
identified systemic risk (pursuant to Measure 2.1) and the overall systemic risk are 
acceptable; and
(3) justify how the use of these tiers and/or other criteria pursuant to point (2) ensures that each 
identified systemic risk (pursuant to Measure 2.1) and the overall systemic risk are 
acceptable.

criteria.title: Post-market monitoring
criteria.requirement: Describe how the framework defines post-market monitoring to gather information relevant to systemic risk assessment and updating, and how independent external evaluators are intended to be enabled under appropriate safeguards, where applicable.
criteria.assessment_question: What post-market monitoring methods are required for assessing and mitigating systemic risk, and under what conditions and safeguards must independent external evaluators be granted access to model versions, chains-of-thought, and safety-reduced model variants, including protections against legal retaliation and responsible vulnerability disclosure timelines?
expected_evidence: The framework describes that post-market monitoring is conducted to gather information about the model’s capabilities, propensities, affordances, and/or effects.
The framework explains that post-market monitoring informs systemic risk acceptability determinations and decisions on framework or report updates.

The framework indicates that a range of post-market monitoring methods may be used, such as collecting end-user feedback, providing reporting or incident channels, engaging with affected stakeholders, monitoring public sources, or supporting independent research.
The framework describes how post-market monitoring applies when the model is integrated into AI systems provided or deployed by the Signatory.
The framework describes whether and under what conditions independent external evaluators are intended to be provided with access to the model for post-market monitoring purposes.

The framework explains the safeguards associated with external evaluator access, such as selection criteria, information security measures, responsible disclosure procedures, and non-retaliation commitments.

Indicative concepts and phrases: post-market monitoring, continuous monitoring, incident reporting, feedback channels, independent external evaluators, evaluator access, safeguards, responsible disclosure, non-retaliation
criteria.reasoning: Indicators present: post-market monitoring purposes, methods, access for independent external evaluators, and safeguards (non-retaliation, selection criteria, information security). Missing: explicit timelines for responsible vulnerability disclosure and defined data-retention/archiving periods for evaluation results/logs. Because these are binary operational requirements, their absence cannot be offset by thematic alignment, yielding NOT_COMPLIANT.
key_aligned_concepts: Post-market monitoring gathers information on model capabilities, propensities, affordances, and effects
Independent external evaluators access to model versions and chains-of-thought under safeguards
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Explicit timelines for responsible vulnerability disclosure
Defined data retention/archiving periods for evaluation results/logs

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: The text requires post-market monitoring to gather information about a model’s capabilities, propensities, affordances, and effects, informs systemic risk acceptability and potential updates, enumerates multiple monitoring methods (e.g., end-user feedback, incident reporting, bug bounties, stakeholder dialogues, public/academic monitoring), applies this to AI systems deployed by Signatories, and permits independent external evaluators access to the most capable version(s) and, where available, its chains-of-thought and safety-reduced variants under safeguarded access with non-retaliation and responsible disclosure provisions.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: The framework aligns with the EU requirement by detailing post-market monitoring purposes, methods, external-evaluator access, and safeguards; it also specifies access modalities and conditions, ensuring safeguards and non-retaliation commitments are in place.

evidence_citations.quote:
Measure 3.5 Post-market monitoring  Signatories will conduct appropriate post-market monitoring to gather information relevant to assessing whether the systemic risk could be determined to not be acceptable (pursuant to Measure 4.1) and to inform whether a Model Report update is necessary (pursuant to Measure 7.6). Further, Signatories will use best efforts to conduct post-market monitoring to gather information relevant to producing estimates of timelines (pursuant to Measure 1.1, point (2)(c)).

To these ends, post-market monitoring will: 
(1) gather information about the model’s capabilities, propensities, affordances, and/or effects; 
(2) take into account the exemplary methods listed below; and 
(3) if Signatories themselves provide and/or deploy AI systems that integrate their own model, include monitoring the model as part of these AI systems.

criteria.title: Acceptance criteria
criteria.requirement: Describe how the framework defines and justifies systemic risk acceptance criteria or tiers for each identified systemic risk, including how acceptability is determined at the individual and overall level and how safety margins are incorporated.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework describe and justify how systemic risk acceptance criteria or tiers are defined for each identified systemic risk, how they are used to determine acceptability at the individual and overall level, and how appropriate safety margins are incorporated?
expected_evidence: The framework describes how systemic risk acceptance is determined for each identified systemic risk.
The framework defines systemic risk acceptance tiers or, where tiers are not suitable and the risk is not a specified systemic risk, alternative acceptance criteria.

The framework explains that acceptance tiers or criteria are measurable and are defined primarily in terms of model capabilities, and may also incorporate model propensities, risk estimates, or other suitable metrics.
The framework indicates that at least one systemic risk tier exists that has not yet been reached by the model.
The framework describes how acceptance criteria or tiers are used to determine acceptability for each systemic risk and for the overall systemic risk.

The framework explains how safety margins are incorporated into acceptance determination, taking into account uncertainty, potential future changes in model capabilities or usage, limitations of risk assessments, and the effectiveness of safety and security mitigations.

Signatories commit to implementing appropriate safety mitigations along the entire model lifecycle, 
as specified in the Measure for this Commitment, to ensure the systemic risks stemming from the 
model are acceptable (pursuant to Commitment 4).  
Measure 5.1 Appropriate safety mitigations 
Signatories will implement safety mitigations that are appropriate, including sufficiently robust under 
adversarial pressure (e.g. fine-tuning attacks or jailbreaking), taking into account the model’s release 
and distribution strategy. 
 
Examples of safety mitigations are:  
(1) filtering and cleaning training data, e.g. data that might result in undesirable model 
propensities such as unfaithful chain-of-thought traces; 
(2) monitoring and filtering the model’s inputs and/or outputs;  
(3) changing the model behaviour in the interests of safety, such as fine-tuning the model to 
refuse certain requests or provide unhelpful responses;  
(4) staging the access to the model, e.g. by limiting API access to vetted users, gradually 
expanding access based on post-market monitoring, and/or not making the model 
parameters publicly available for download initially;  
(5) offering tools for other actors to use to mitigate the systemic risks stemming from the model;  
(6) techniques that provide high-assurance quantitative safety guarantees concerning the 
model’s behaviour;

Measure 1.3 Updating the Framework  
Signatories will update the Framework as appropriate, including without undue delay after a 
Framework assessment (specified in the following paragraphs), to ensure the information in Measure 
1.1 is kept up-to-date and the Framework is at least state-of-the-art. For any update of the

LEGAL TEXT: Article 55(1) and recital 114 AI Act 
Signatories commit to implementing appropriate safety mitigations along the entire model lifecycle, 
as specified in the Measure for this Commitment, to ensure the systemic risks stemming from the 
model are acceptable (pursuant to Commitment 4).  
Measure 5.1 Appropriate safety mitigations 
Signatories will implement safety mitigations that are appropriate, including sufficiently robust under 
adversarial pressure (e.g. fine-tuning attacks or jailbreaking), taking into account the model’s release 
and distribution strategy. 
 
Examples of safety mitigations are:  
(1) filtering and cleaning training data, e.g. data that might result in undesirable model 
propensities such as unfaithful chain-of-thought traces; 
(2) monitoring and filtering the model’s inputs and/or outputs;  
(3) changing the model behaviour in the interests of safety, such as fine-tuning the model to 
refuse certain requests or provide unhelpful responses;  
(4) staging the access to the model, e.g. by limiting API access to vetted users, gradually 
expanding access based on post-market monitoring, and/or not making the model 
parameters publicly available for download initially;  
(5) offering tools for other actors to use to mitigate the systemic risks stemming from the model;  
(6) techniques that provide high-assurance quantitative safety guarantees concerning the 
model’s behaviour;

If no independent external evaluator was involved, the Model Report provides a justification referencing the applicable exception conditions (e.g., similarly safe or safer model, or inability to appoint qualified evaluators despite early search efforts).

If at least one independent external evaluator was involved, the Model Report explains the choice of evaluator with reference to qualification criteria (e.g., domain expertise, technical evaluation experience, appropriate security protocols, confidentiality protections).

Framework, Signatories will include a changelog, describing how and why the Framework has been 
updated, along with a version number and the date of change. 
Signatories will conduct an appropriate Framework assessment, if they have reasonable grounds to 
believe that the adequacy of their Framework and/or their adherence thereto has been or will be 
materially undermined, or every 12 months starting from their placing of the model on the market, 
whichever is sooner. Examples of such grounds are:  
(1) how the Signatories develop models will change materially, which can be reasonably foreseen 
to lead to the systemic risks stemming from at least one of their models not being acceptable; 
(2) serious incidents and/or near misses involving their models or similar models that are likely 
to indicate that the systemic risks stemming from at least one of their models are not 
acceptable have occurred; and/or 
(3) the systemic risks stemming from at least one of their models have changed or are likely to 
change materially, e.g. safety and/or security mitigations have become or are likely to 
become materially less effective, or at least one of their models has developed or is likely to 
develop materially changed capabilities and/or propensities.

not changed since they have last provided the AI Office with the Model Report, or update thereof; (2) 
they will place a more capable model on the market in less than a month; and/or (3) the model is 
considered similarly safe or safer (pursuant to Appendix 2.2) for each identified systemic risk 
(pursuant to Measure 2.1).  
The updated Model Report will contain:  
(1) the updated information specified in Measures 7.1 to 7.5 based on the results of the full 
systemic risk assessment and mitigation process (pursuant to Measure 1.2, third paragraph); 
and 
(2) a changelog, describing how and why the Model Report has been updated, along with a 
version number and the date of change. 
Measure 7.7 Model Report notifications  
Signatories will provide the AI Office with access to the Model Report (without redactions, unless they 
are required by national security laws to which Signatories are subject) by the time they place a model 
on the market, e.g. through a publicly accessible link or through a sufficiently secure channel specified 
by the AI Office. If a Model Report is updated, Signatories will provide the AI Office with access to the 
updated Model Report (without redactions, unless they are required by national security laws to 
which Signatories are subject) within five business days of a confirmed update.

Signatories commit to: (1) defining clear responsibilities for managing the systemic risks stemming 
from their models across all levels of the organisation (as specified in Measure 8.1); (2) allocating 
appropriate resources to actors who have been assigned responsibilities for managing systemic risk

Commitment 10 Additional documentation and 
transparency 
 
LEGAL TEXT: Articles 53(1)(a) and 55(1) AI Act 
Signatories commit to documenting the implementation of this Chapter (as specified in Measure 10.1) 
and publish summarised versions of their Framework and Model Reports as necessary (as specified 
in Measure 10.2). 
Measure 10.1 Additional documentation 
Signatories will draw up and keep up-to-date the following information for the purpose of providing 
it to the AI Office upon request: 
(1) a detailed description of the model’s architecture; 
(2) a detailed description of how the model is integrated into AI systems, explaining how 
software components build or feed into each other and integrate into the overall processing, 
insofar as the Signatory is aware of such information; 
(3) a detailed description of the model evaluations conducted pursuant to this Chapter, including 
their results and strategies; and 
(4) a detailed description of the safety mitigations implemented (pursuant to Commitment 5). 
Documentation will be retained at least 10 years after the model has been placed on the market. 
Further, Signatories will keep track of the following information, to the extent it is not already covered 
by the first paragraph, for the purpose of evidencing adherence to this Chapter to the AI Office upon 
request: 
(1) their processes, measures, and key decisions that form part of their systemic risk assessment 
and mitigation; and

third paragraph), including that the systemic risks stemming from the model have been 
determined to be acceptable (pursuant to Commitment 4), and the AI Office has received its 
Model Report (pursuant to Commitment 7); 
(2) the Signatory has sufficient visibility into the model’s characteristics such as relevant 
architectural details, capabilities, propensities, affordances, and safety mitigations. Such 
visibility is assumed for all models developed by the Signatory itself and for all models for 
which the Signatory has access to all information that would be necessary for the Signatory 
to complete the full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process (pursuant to Measure 
1.2, third paragraph), including the model parameters; and 
(3) there are no other reasonable grounds to believe that the systemic risks stemming from the 
model are not acceptable.

criteria.title: Responsibilities
criteria.requirement: Describe whether and how the framework defines clear responsibilities for managing systemic risks, including systemic risk oversight, ownership, support and monitoring, and assurance, and how these responsibilities are allocated across organisational governance levels.
criteria.assessment_question: How must signatories assign systemic risk oversight, ownership, support and monitoring, and assurance responsibilities across the management body in its supervisory and executive functions, operational teams, and internal and external assurance providers, including role-specific requirements such as separation from core business activities and cascading responsibility structures for SMEs and SMCs?
expected_evidence: The framework explicitly defines responsibilities for systemic risk oversight, ownership, support and monitoring, and assurance.
The framework describes how systemic risk oversight is assigned to a supervisory or otherwise independent governance function.
The framework describes how systemic risk ownership is assigned to executive-level functions responsible for risk-producing activities.
The framework describes how systemic risk support and monitoring is assigned to functions that are organisationally independent from core business activities.
The framework describes how systemic risk assurance is provided to a supervisory or independent body, including internal and, where applicable, external assurance.
The framework acknowledges proportional allocation of responsibilities based on organisational size and complexity (e.g. SMEs or SMCs).
Indicative concepts and phrases: systemic risk oversight, systemic risk ownership, support and monitoring, assurance, governance levels, supervisory function, executive function, independence
criteria.reasoning: All indicators are present in the text: systemic risk oversight allocated to supervisory/independent bodies; systemic risk ownership to executive-level functions; systemic risk support/monitoring to independent functions; systemic risk assurance to supervisory/independent bodies (including internal and external assurance); proportional allocation for SMEs/SMCs; and resource allocation considerations. No operational gaps or missing structural indicators were identified.

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: Yes; the retrieved text explicitly defines and allocates systemic risk oversight to supervisory/independent bodies, systemic risk ownership to executive-level functions responsible for risk-producing activities, systemic risk support and monitoring to functions independent from core business, and systemic risk assurance to internal/external assurance providers, including separation from core activities and proportionate structures for SMEs/SMCs.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: The text aligns with the EU requirement by outlining explicit governance-level allocations for oversight, ownership, support/monitoring, and assurance, including independence from core activities and proportionate considerations for smaller entities.

evidence_citations.quote: (1) Systemic risk oversight: The responsibility for overseeing the Signatory’s systemic risk management processes and measures has been assigned to a specific committee of the management body in its supervisory function (e.g. a risk committee or audit committee) or one or multiple suitable independent bodies (such as councils or boards). For Signatories that are SMEs or SMCs, this responsibility may be primarily assigned to an individual member of the management body in its supervisory function.
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Directly establishes who holds systemic risk oversight and accommodates SMEs/SMCs.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: Systemic risk oversight defined and allocated to supervisory/independent bodies (including SME/SMC adaptation).

evidence_citations.quote: (3) Systemic risk support and monitoring: The responsibility for supporting and monitoring the Signatory’s systemic risk management processes and measures, including conducting risk assessments, has been assigned to at least one member of the management body in its executive function (e.g. a Chief Risk Officer or a Vice President, Safety & Security Framework). This member(s) must not also be responsible for the Signatory’s core business activities that may produce systemic risk (e.g. research and product development). For Signatories that are SMEs or SMCs, there is at least one individual in the management body in its executive function tasked with supporting and monitoring the Signatory’s systemic risk assessment and mitigation processes and measures.
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Shows independence from core activities and dedicated risk-support roles.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: Systemic risk support and monitoring assigned to executive-level function independent from core business (including SME/SMC adaptation).

evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Directly demonstrates cross-level allocation and inclusion of assurance mechanisms.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: Allocation of systemic risk ownership, support/monitoring, and assurance across governance levels (supervisory, executive, operational, assurance providers) with independence considerations.

evidence_citations.quote: Measure 8.2 Allocation of appropriate resources Signatories will ensure that their management bodies oversee the allocation of resources to those who have been assigned responsibilities (pursuant to Measure 8.1) that are appropriate for the systemic risks stemming from their models. The allocation of such resources will include: (1) human resources; (2) financial resources; (3) access to information and knowledge; and (4) computational resources.
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Operationalizes governance by ensuring adequate resources for systemic risk responsibilities.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: Resource allocation to responsible roles across governance levels (supporting the governance structure).

Measure 8.3 Promotion of a healthy risk culture 
Signatories will promote a healthy risk culture and take appropriate measures to ensure that actors 
who have been assigned responsibilities for managing the systemic risks stemming from their models 
(pursuant to Measure 8.1) take a reasoned and balanced approach to systemic risk. 
Examples of indicators of a healthy risk culture for the purpose of this Measure are: 
(1) setting the tone for a healthy systemic risk culture from the top, e.g. by the leadership clearly 
communicating the Signatory’s Framework to staff; 
(2) allowing clear communication and challenge of decisions concerning systemic risk; 
(3) setting incentives and affording sufficient independence of staff involved in systemic risk 
assessment and mitigation to discourage excessive systemic-risk-taking and encourage an 
unbiased assessment of the systemic risks stemming from their models; 
(4) anonymous surveys find that staff are comfortable raising concerns about systemic risks, are 
aware of channels for doing so, and understand the Signatory’s Framework; 
(5) internal reporting channels are actively used and reports are acted upon appropriately; 
(6) annually informing workers of the Signatory’s whistleblower protection policy and making 
such policy readily available to workers such as by publishing it on their website; and/or 
(7) not retaliating in any form, including any direct or indirect detrimental action such as

(1) a description and justification of the trigger points and their usage, at which the Signatories 
will conduct additional lighter-touch model evaluations along the entire model lifecycle, as 
specified in Measure 1.2, second paragraph, point (1)(a);
(2) for the Signatories’ determination of whether systemic risk is considered acceptable, as 
specified in Commitment 4: 
(a) a description and justification of the systemic risk acceptance criteria, including the 
systemic risk tiers, and their usage as specified in Measure 4.1; 
(b) a high-level description of what safety and security mitigations Signatories would 
need to implement once each systemic risk tier is reached;

Signatories will describe and justify (in the Framework pursuant to Measure 1.1, point (2)(a)) how 
they will determine whether the systemic risks stemming from the model are acceptable. To do so,

not suitable for the systemic risk and the systemic risk is not a specified systemic risk

identified systemic risk (pursuant to Measure 2.1) and the overall systemic risk are 
acceptable; and
(3) justify how the use of these tiers and/or other criteria pursuant to point (2) ensures that each 
identified systemic risk (pursuant to Measure 2.1) and the overall systemic risk are 
acceptable.

Commitment 9 Serious incident reporting  
 
LEGAL TEXT: Article 55(1), and recitals 114 and 115 AI Act 
Signatories commit to implementing appropriate processes and measures for keeping track of, 
documenting, and reporting to the AI Office and, as applicable, to national competent authorities, 
without undue delay relevant information about serious incidents along the entire model lifecycle 
and possible corrective measures to address them, as specified in the Measures of this Commitment. 
Further, Signatories commit to providing resourcing of such processes and measures appropriate for 
the severity of the serious incident and the degree of involvement of their model.  
Measure 9.1 Methods for serious incident identification 
Signatories will consider the exemplary methods in Measure 3.5 to keep track of relevant information 
about serious incidents. Additionally, Signatories will:

Signatories will consider the exemplary methods in Measure 3.5 to keep track of relevant information 
about serious incidents. Additionally, Signatories will: 
(1) review other sources of information, such as police and media reports, posts on social media, 
research papers, and incident databases; and
(2) facilitate the reporting of relevant information about serious incidents by downstream 
modifiers, downstream providers, users, and other third parties to: 
(a) the Signatory; or 
(b) the AI Office and, as applicable, national competent authorities; 
by informing such third parties of direct reporting channels, if available, without prejudice to 
any of their reporting obligations under Article 73 AI Act. 
Measure 9.2 Relevant information for serious incident tracking, documentation, and 
reporting 
Signatories will keep track of, document, and report to the AI Office and, as applicable, to national 
competent authorities, at least the following information to the best of their knowledge, redacted 
to the extent necessary to comply with other Union law applicable to such information: 
(1) the start and end dates of the serious incident, or best approximations thereof if the precise 
dates are unclear; 
(2) the resulting harm and the victim or affected group of the serious incident;  
(3) the chain of events that (directly or indirectly) led to the serious incident;  
(4) the model involved in the serious incident;

incident reports. The level of detail in serious incident reports will be appropriate for the severity of 
the incident. 
Measure 9.3 Reporting timelines 
Signatories will provide the information in points (1) to (7) of Measure 9.2 in an initial report that is 
submitted to the AI Office and, as applicable, to national competent authorities, at the following 
points in time, save in exceptional circumstances, if the involvement of their model (directly or 
indirectly) led to: 
(1) a serious and irreversible disruption of the management or operation of critical 
infrastructure, or if the Signatories establish or suspect with reasonable likelihood such a 
causal relationship between their model and the disruption, not later than two days after the 
Signatories become aware of the involvement of their model in the incident;
(2) a serious cybersecurity breach, including the (self-)exfiltration of model weights and 
cyberattacks, or if the Signatories establish or suspect with reasonable likelihood such a 
causal relationship between their model and the breach, not later than five days after the 
Signatories become aware of the involvement of their model in the incident; 
(3) a death of a person, or if the Signatories establish or suspect with reasonable likelihood such 
a causal relationship between their model and the death, not later than 10 days after the 
Signatories become aware of the involvement of their model in the incident; and

doubt, in good faith in light of: (1) the probability and severity of harm pursuant to the 
definition of ‘risk’ in Article 3(2) AI Act; and (2) the definition of ‘systemic risk’ in Article 3(65) 
AI Act. The Signatories recognise that this Chapter is to be interpreted in conjunction and in 
accordance with any AI Office guidance on the AI Act. 
(j) Serious Incident Reporting. The Signatories recognise that the reporting of a serious incident 
is not an admission of wrongdoing. Further, they recognise that relevant information about 
serious incidents cannot be kept track of, documented, and reported at the model level only 
in retrospect after a serious incident has occurred. The information that could directly or 
indirectly lead up to such an event is often dispersed and may be lost, overwritten, or 
fragmented by the time Signatories become aware of a serious incident. This justifies the 
establishment of processes and measures to keep track of and document relevant 
information before serious incidents occur.

criteria.requirement: The framework defines mandatory severity-based reporting timelines for serious incidents involving the model, including differentiated deadlines for initial reports based on incident type, requirements for periodic intermediate updates for unresolved incidents, and submission of a final report after incident resolution.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework specify clearly differentiated reporting timelines for serious incidents (including specific deadlines for initial notification based on severity), periodic intermediate updates for unresolved incidents, and a final report after resolution?
expected_evidence: The framework defines categories of serious incidents (e.g., critical infrastructure disruption, cybersecurity breach, death, serious harm to health, fundamental rights, property or environment).
The framework associates specific deadlines for initial reporting following awareness of a serious incident (e.g., two days, five days, ten days, fifteen days depending on severity).
The framework clarifies that reporting is triggered when the organisation becomes aware of the involvement of its model, including cases of reasonable suspicion of causal linkage.
The framework specifies periodic intermediate updates for unresolved serious incidents (e.g., at least every four weeks after the initial report).
The framework defines a deadline for submitting a final report after resolution of the serious incident (e.g., within 60 days after resolution).
The framework allows aggregation of multiple similar serious incidents within defined reporting timelines while respecting the earliest applicable deadline.

Signatories commit to implementing appropriate processes and measures for keeping track of, 
documenting, and reporting to the AI Office and, as applicable, to national competent authorities, 
without undue delay relevant information about serious incidents along the entire model lifecycle 
and possible corrective measures to address them, as specified in the Measures of this Commitment. 
Further, Signatories commit to providing resourcing of such processes and measures appropriate for 
the severity of the serious incident and the degree of involvement of their model.

Measure 9.3 Reporting timelines 
Signatories will provide the information in points (1) to (7) of Measure 9.2 in an initial report that is 
submitted to the AI Office and, as applicable, to national competent authorities, at the following 
points in time, save in exceptional circumstances, if the involvement of their model (directly or 
indirectly) led to: 
(1) a serious and irreversible disruption of the management or operation of critical 
infrastructure, or if the Signatories establish or suspect with reasonable likelihood such a 
causal relationship between their model and the disruption, not later than two days after the 
Signatories become aware of the involvement of their model in the incident;
(2) a serious cybersecurity breach, including the (self-)exfiltration of model weights and 
cyberattacks, or if the Signatories establish or suspect with reasonable likelihood such a 
causal relationship between their model and the breach, not later than five days after the 
Signatories become aware of the involvement of their model in the incident; 
(3) a death of a person, or if the Signatories establish or suspect with reasonable likelihood such 
a causal relationship between their model and the death, not later than 10 days after the 
Signatories become aware of the involvement of their model in the incident; and

Signatories become aware of the involvement of their model in the incident; and 
(4) serious harm to a person’s health (mental and/or physical), an infringement of obligations 
under Union law intended to protect fundamental rights, and/or serious harm to property or 
the environment, or if the Signatories establish or suspect with reasonable likelihood such a 
causal relationship between their model and the harms or infringements, not later than 15 
days after the Signatories become aware of the involvement of their model in the incident. 
For unresolved serious incidents, Signatories will update the information in their initial report and 
add further information required by Measure 9.2, as available, in an intermediate report that is 
submitted to the AI Office and, as applicable, to national competent authorities, at least every four 
weeks after the initial report. 
Signatories will submit a final report, covering all the information required by Measure 9.2, to the AI 
Office and, as applicable, to national competent authorities, not later than 60 days after the serious 
incident has been resolved. 
If multiple similar serious incidents occur within the reporting timelines, Signatories may include them 
in the report(s) of the first serious incident, while respecting the timelines for reporting for the first 
serious incident. 
Measure 9.4 Retention period

Signatories will consider the exemplary methods in Measure 3.5 to keep track of relevant information 
about serious incidents. Additionally, Signatories will: 
(1) review other sources of information, such as police and media reports, posts on social media, 
research papers, and incident databases; and
(2) facilitate the reporting of relevant information about serious incidents by downstream 
modifiers, downstream providers, users, and other third parties to: 
(a) the Signatory; or 
(b) the AI Office and, as applicable, national competent authorities; 
by informing such third parties of direct reporting channels, if available, without prejudice to 
any of their reporting obligations under Article 73 AI Act. 
Measure 9.2 Relevant information for serious incident tracking, documentation, and 
reporting 
Signatories will keep track of, document, and report to the AI Office and, as applicable, to national 
competent authorities, at least the following information to the best of their knowledge, redacted 
to the extent necessary to comply with other Union law applicable to such information: 
(1) the start and end dates of the serious incident, or best approximations thereof if the precise 
dates are unclear; 
(2) the resulting harm and the victim or affected group of the serious incident;  
(3) the chain of events that (directly or indirectly) led to the serious incident;  
(4) the model involved in the serious incident;
